extracted.intended_audience: computer science students, programmers writing literate programs, and academics who referee or prepare user manuals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing literate programs (module naming, module size, exposition, variable naming, typography, user manuals) and for refereeing academic papers (originality, constructive criticism, technical improvement, standards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural order of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Present program constructs in the same order the creator made decisions about them; prefer the 'natural order' of exposition which matches the natural reading/writing order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don felt throughout composition there was a natural order of exposition and that the best way to present program constructs is to follow the order in which decisions were made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent personification/voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a personification for program behavior (e.g., 'we', 'it', or 'I') and be consistent throughout documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don favours 'we'; some (e.g., Dijkstra) dislike anthropomorphization. Consistency matters for clarity and reader conceptualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module naming: imperatives vs descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Name modules performing actions with imperatives (e.g., 'Store the word in the dictionary') and name declarative text/listing modules with descriptors (e.g., 'Procedures for sorting').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize the first letter of a module name; choose naming form appropriate to module function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readable identifier formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid awkward internal capitalization (e.g., 'FindinNew Word3'); use readable conventions such as short underscores to conjoin words or long descriptive identifiers where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WEB allows underscores to conjoin words but TANGLE removes underscores for some targets; early compilers used very long identifiers (~40 chars) with clear meaning even without comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module description: high-level, informal, intuitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Each module should contain an informal but clear description conveying the intuition of what the module does; avoid play-by-play stepping through of the algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple stepping through does not qualify; aim for a high-level account that helps the reader understand the overall behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module length and modularization
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep modules short and manageable (Don suggests about a dozen lines); break large modules into smaller pieces so complex things are tractable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The philosophy behind WEB is to break a complex thing into tractable parts; cut offending specimens into several pieces to improve manageability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'engineerese' and maintain readable prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write descriptive text as a run-on 'engineerese' without punctuation; use proper punctuation and readable sentences for good documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjunction-only text without punctuation may work for stream-of-consciousness literature but not for documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drop obsolete conventions when changing style
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not carry over unnecessary older conventions into new styles (e.g., adding comments after each 'end' in WEB when it's unnecessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you change style you needn't carry excess baggage along; follow conventions appropriate to the new format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Block-structuring convention consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Put begins/ends inside the called modules rather than in the calling module; be consistent with block-structuring conventions to avoid bugs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing the two conventions (placing begins/ends in caller vs callee) can cause appalling bugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable naming: part-of-speech discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Use nouns for data (variables) and verbs for procedures; let the function determine the part of speech—'place' (noun) might be better than a verb-name for a data marker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'Truth in Naming' improves readability and signals intended usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable declaration practice
rubrics_metrics.description: When declaring variables (possible at any point in WEB), add at least a cursory explanatory comment; keep declarations close to their use or distribute local variables as exposition proceeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let variables in the module title correspond to the local parameters in the module itself; distributing local variables fits WEB philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use italics for variable names in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Typeset variable names in italics when they appear in comments to distinguish them from surrounding prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don recommended this as a good practice for clarity in documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic conventions for data and numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use typewriter font for hexadecimal numbers or data-as-appears-in-files; use 'x' for multiplication rather than asterisks since typeset asterisks may align poorly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave decimal numerals in normal type; this provides subliminal type-checking and clearer presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with quotation marks and symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for differences between opening/closing quotes (typesetting vs ASCII) and avoid starting sentences with a symbol; rewrite such sentences for readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different languages/styles use different quote conventions; starting a sentence with a symbol (e.g., 'data assumes that...') is discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology consistency between docs and code
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the same words in documentation as in the formal program; do not use two different terms for the same concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistent terminology will confuse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group related specialized routines in documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep specialized routines (e.g., heap routines) together in the text so they can be read as a group while the details are fresh in the reader's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WEB's flexible ordering allows grouping such routines regardless of top-down/bottom-up constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use displayed equations in comments where helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: WEB allows displayed equations in comments; use this feature when mathematical checks or explanations (e.g., triangle inequality checks) benefit the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked example: checking road-vs-great-circle distances can be illustrated with displayed equations in comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macrology: limited, pragmatic macros
rubrics_metrics.description: Use macros (WEB macros limited to about one parameter) pragmatically to extend language capabilities without needing a complex parser; simulate multi-parameter macros when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include work-arounds for Pascal limitations (e.g., defining string_type(#) to create packed arrays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Module titles and parameter correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Let variables in the module title correspond to the module's local parameters to maintain clarity between the title and implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps the reader map exposition to code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module text should include illustrative data samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a typewriter font to show how data actually appears in files when characterizing program input and output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes the specification concrete and helps readers understand expected formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize only first word in module titles (headline style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid capitalizing the first letter of every word in module titles; better to follow headline conventions by capitalizing only the first word (or use newspaper style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fully capitalizing every word looks unnatural and affects readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: User manual: avoid jargon and explain technical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Write user manuals for naive users: avoid technical terms (e.g., 'menu', 'scrolling', 'reverse video') or explain them clearly and use intuitive wording (e.g., 'hit return' rather than 'enter').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don's wife often found such jargon meaningless; technical words familiar to CS people may be opaque to typical users.

rubrics_metrics.name: User manual: tell users how to recover/exit
rubrics_metrics.description: Always explain how a user can 'get out of a mess' or exit if they do something wrong; do not assume users know how to stop using the program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a one-line description of how to EXIT may still be jargon—make it truly accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: User manual: clear, skimmable organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a good overview, step-by-step descriptions, crisp sentences, helpful redundancy, and diagrams so the manual is easy to skim and use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People often start reading in the middle; structure and redundancy help them find needed information quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: User manual: use diagrams, keyboard maps, and icons
rubrics_metrics.description: Include keyboard diagrams, symbols to indicate control keys, and icons for actions (scroll up/down/left/right) to demonstrate interaction clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize that control keys must be held while typing another key; use icons to clarify non-obvious actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: User interface: mnemonic and consistent command keys
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose command keys that are mnemonic and consistent (e.g., use OPTION-N to return to normal rather than reusing OPTION-B to toggle bold), and prefer predictable mnemonics (Option-R for reverse video).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid symmetric toggles that are not mnemonic; defaulting to previous line style parameters is preferable to re-asking every time.

rubrics_metrics.name: User manual: offer interactive demos/help
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow the user to type '?' or similar to get an online demonstration to avoid long arcane descriptions and keep the manual terse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An animated or interactive demo can be worth a paragraph and spares clumsy textual explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: User manual: avoid misleading marketing claims and ALL CAPS
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make grand claims like 'very easy to use' that can insult users; avoid using ALL CAPS in instructions as they come across as alarm signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reassuring, clear language (friendly comments like 'Good luck!' can be appropriate if not misleading).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliographic thoroughness and proofreading
rubrics_metrics.description: Include adequate bibliographic details (e.g., exact conference location/date) because libraries may index conferences by city; meticulously proofread galley proofs and correct typographic/notation issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don noted many bibliographies contain errors; proofreaders' symbols and attention to galley changes are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing primary criterion: originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the material is a genuine advance on previous work; originality should be the first criterion for referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees are expert witnesses who determine whether a paper merits publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing responsibility: serve authors and readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should see their primary responsibility as to authors and readers (helping improve exposition and technical quality), not merely to editors or career advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don urged referees to help authors improve writing and technical content; act as teachers rather than anonymous critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee conduct: constructive criticism and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid tasteless anonymous attacks; provide constructive, respectful criticism aimed at improving the author's future work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-critical or rude comments anger authors and teach them nothing; be cooperative rather than legalistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee contribution: provide references and technical fixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply references to related work the author may be unaware of and, where possible, contribute technical improvements or corrected proofs (sometimes anonymously acknowledged).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees can materially improve the technical quality of a paper; some have their contributions acknowledged in footnotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee checklist: essential paper components
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper with the given title should contain expected elements such as (1) a complete algorithm, (2) a proof or convincing explanation of correctness, and (3) a statement of limitations/applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One referee's general comment listed these as a minimal set of expectations for algorithm papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee selectivity: choose journals with good referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should submit to journals known to have the best referees rather than to journals with lenient editors; rigorous refereeing helps authors learn if they've made a real contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A journal's value lies in its referees' quality; better referees provide more reliable evaluations and useful feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing focus: content over grammar unless substantive
rubrics_metrics.description: If the content of a paper is obviously bad, do not waste time on grammar; but for substantive papers, help ensure both content and exposition are as good as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don would not focus on grammar for worthless content but would for papers with real contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing reports: use clear recommendation categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should assign overall ratings (accept, accept with minor/major modifications, reject) and may suggest alternative, less-prestigious journals for rejected work as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such downward filtering allows papers to find an appropriate outlet even if not suitable for the first-choice journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid facile generalizations in reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not offer mechanical or merely formal generalizations that add no new insight; constructive, insightful feedback is preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polya's term 'facile generalizations' describes comments that are mechanical manipulations without creating new insight.
